title: Just 12 Weeks of Time-Restricted Eating Can Keep Weight Off for a Full Year, a New Study Finds
excerpt: A randomised trial from Spain shows that limiting meals to an eight-hour window produces durable weight loss regardless of whether you eat early or late — a flexible strategy that could reshape how South Asians manage obesity.
body:
The promise of intermittent fasting has always carried an asterisk: *does the weight stay off once you stop?* A new randomised controlled trial from the University of Granada, published this week in *Clinical Nutrition*, offers the strongest evidence yet that it can — and that the timing of your meals matters far less than whether you stick to a narrower eating window.

## The Study

Researchers enrolled overweight and obese adults and randomly assigned them to one of three time-restricted eating (TRE) regimens for 12 weeks: an early eating window (roughly 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.), a late window (roughly noon to 8 p.m.), or a self-selected eight-hour window chosen by the participants themselves. Crucially, no group was asked to count calories or follow a prescribed diet — they simply compressed their meals into eight hours.

All three groups lost a clinically meaningful amount of weight over the 12-week intervention. But the headline result came from the 12-month follow-up: participants were tracked for a full year after the intervention ended, with no further guidance or coaching. The researchers found that weight loss persisted across all three groups. Moreover, roughly one in three participants chose to continue practising intermittent fasting on their own during the follow-up year — a telling sign that the approach was not just effective but liveable.

"A very positive finding is that one in three people decided to continue practising intermittent fasting on their own during that year of follow-up, suggesting that it is a relatively easy habit to integrate into daily life," the researchers noted.

## Why It Matters



> **"Crucially, no group was asked to count calories or follow a prescribed diet — they simply compressed their meals into eight hours."**


Most diets fail not in the losing phase but in the keeping-it-off phase. Weight regain within 12 to 24 months is the norm, not the exception, for calorie-restriction approaches. The Granada trial is one of the first randomised studies to show that TRE — specifically, an eight-hour eating window maintained for just 12 weeks — produces durable results without requiring participants to weigh food, track macros, or attend counselling sessions.

The finding that early, late, and self-selected windows were all effective is significant. Previous research had suggested that eating earlier in the day might confer extra metabolic benefits because of circadian rhythm alignment. While that may be true at the margins, the practical takeaway from this trial is simpler: *pick whichever window fits your life, and you'll likely still benefit.*


![University of Granada — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c1/Hospital_Real_de_Granada_-_Espa%C3%B1a.jpg/3840px-Hospital_Real_de_Granada_-_Espa%C3%B1a.jpg)


## The South Asian Context

For Indian-origin communities, the relevance is direct. South Asians develop insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes at lower body weights and younger ages than most other populations. Metabolic syndrome — the cluster of elevated blood sugar, blood pressure, waist circumference, and triglycerides — is estimated to affect anywhere from 25% to 40% of urban Indians, depending on the study.

Standard weight-management advice often clashes with cultural eating patterns. Extended family dinners, late-night chai, weekend social eating, and religious fasting traditions all shape when and how South Asians eat. The finding that a self-selected window works just as well as a rigidly timed one means that a Diwali host or a Ramadan observer could potentially adapt TRE around their existing habits rather than abandoning them.

There is also a practical point for NRIs working long hours in demanding professional roles. An eight-hour eating window that begins with a late breakfast and ends with an early dinner — or begins with lunch and ends with a late dinner — can slot into a typical workday without requiring special meal prep or supplements.

## What This Does Not Mean

The study does not prove that intermittent fasting is superior to other weight-loss methods. It does not show that TRE reverses diabetes or prevents heart disease on its own. And it was conducted on overweight and obese adults in Spain — a population that is metabolically different from South Asians in some respects, though the core mechanisms of insulin sensitivity and calorie balance are broadly shared.

Researchers also caution that people on diabetes medications, pregnant women, and those with a history of eating disorders should consult a doctor before adopting any fasting regimen.

## The Bigger Picture

The study adds to a growing body of evidence — including a *Nature Aging* paper showing that eight-hour TRE extends healthspan in mice — that meal timing is a meaningful lever for metabolic health. The practical appeal of TRE is that it asks for one behavioural change (compress your eating window) rather than the dozens of micro-decisions that calorie counting demands.

For a community with among the highest metabolic risk profiles in the world, that simplicity may be exactly the advantage that makes the difference between a diet that lasts 12 weeks and one that lasts a lifetime.
